Ike is a PhD student in the [UKRI AI Centre for Doctoral Training in Practice-Oriented Artificial Intelligence](https://www.bristol.ac.uk/cdt/practice-oriented-ai/) at the University of Bristol. His research focuses on multimodal perception, computer vision, and spatiotemporal learning for autonomous systems. He is particularly interested in developing AI systems that combine visual and onboard sensor information to understand complex and dynamic environments.

His current research explores UAV–environment interaction, using video and aircraft telemetry to understand and model how unmanned aerial vehicles interact with challenging atmospheric environments. His recent work investigates UAV–volcanic plume interactions, including multimodal learning of the different stages of interaction and, more broadly, how these interactions can be represented and modelled for autonomous perception.

Before joining the University of Bristol, Ike conducted research at the University of Tartu spanning autonomous systems, artificial intelligence, computer vision, and spacecraft control. Working with Prof. Andris Slavinskis and Prof. Gholamreza Anbarjafari (Shahab), his research included fault-tolerant spacecraft attitude control, robotic perception, and computer vision. His broader work in autonomous systems has also included UAV development, autopilot systems, and flight testing. He also completed an MSc in Robotics and Computer Engineering at the University of Tartu, graduating *cum laude* (with distinction).

---

## Research

Ike's research interests lie at the intersection of multimodal AI, computer vision, robotics, and autonomous systems. His current interests include:

- Multimodal perception and sensor fusion
- Computer vision and video understanding
- Spatiotemporal learning
- UAV and autonomous-system perception
- Dynamic environment and interaction modelling
- Robotics and intelligent autonomous systems

## Featured Work

### Multimodal Spatiotemporal Learning of UAV–Environment Interactions

Understanding UAV interactions with complex atmospheric environments using onboard video and aircraft telemetry.

The work studies temporally structured UAV–volcanic plume interactions — **approaching, entering, inside, and exiting** — and investigates visual, telemetry-based, and multimodal learning approaches for autonomous perception.
